question: Move the AED at P.S. 184M Shuang Wen into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 184M Shuang Wen (School, ZIP 10002) has a registered AED at "Front Entrance".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.21 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 5 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 5 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists FDNY EMS Station 4, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 163 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving P.S. 184M's AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a genuine gap in emergency access. The school's current hours mean the AED is unreachable during 113 of 168 weekly hours when students aren't present [E3]. More critically, the area experienced an expected 1.21 cardiac-arrest calls annually during times when every nearby AED was closed [E4]—ranking fifth among NYC schools for this vulnerability. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED correlates with 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. While an FDNY station 163 meters away offers an alternative [E8], a street-wall cabinet would eliminate response delays and ensure consistent availability for the neighborhood's actual call patterns.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: Before committing resources to a new cabinet, we should exhaust cheaper alternatives. The fire station 163 meters away already operates 24/7 and could host an AED at minimal cost [E8]—we don't know the cabinet expense or vandalism risk here [E9]. The expected 1.21 annual calls [E4] is modest; we lack the actual call locations within the ZIP to confirm they're closer to the school than to Station 4 [E9]. The survival research [E7] is compelling, but applies to shockable arrests—we don't know if those 1.21 calls were shockable. Test the fire station option first.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic's point about the fire station deserves serious consideration, but distance matters more than it appears. While Station 4 at 163 meters is closer than many alternatives, the two-minute walking radius from P.S. 184M is roughly 240 meters—meaning the school location serves a different part of the neighborhood. Critically, we know the area experienced 1.21 expected cardiac-arrest calls annually during hours when every reachable AED was closed [E4], yet we don't know whether those calls clustered near the school or near the fire station [E9]. A street-wall cabinet at the school would guarantee coverage for whichever side of the zone the calls actually occur. Testing the fire station first risks another year without 24/7 access for calls that may be geographically closer to P.S. 184M.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate makes a fair point about geographic uncertainty, but it cuts both ways. We genuinely don't know whether those 1.21 annual calls cluster near the school or the fire station [E9]. That same uncertainty argues for testing the cheaper option first: placing an AED at Station 4, which already operates 24/7 and sits only 163 meters away [E8]. If calls prove closer to the school after a trial period, the cabinet investment becomes justified by real data rather than assumption. We also lack critical information on cabinet costs and vandalism risk [E9], which could be substantial. Given the modest call volume and an existing 24/7 facility nearby, the fire station pilot is the prudent path forward.

verdict.summary: Data supports 24/7 access need (1.21 annual calls during closure hours, rank 5 of 100 schools), but geographic uncertainty and cheaper alternative warrant testing FDNY Station 4 placement first before street-wall cabinet investment.
verdict.strongestFor: Expected 1.21 annual cardiac-arrest calls occur when all nearby AEDs closed [E4]; 66.5% survival with bystander shock versus 43.0% without [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: FDNY Station 4 operates 24/7 at 163 m away [E8]; actual call locations within ZIP unknown [E9]; cabinet costs and vandalism risk undetermined [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Pilot 24/7 AED placement at FDNY Station 4 for 6 months; track call locations and response times to determine if school-wall cabinet is subsequently justified.
